title: Unbiased Private Estimators by Postprocessing the Discrete Laplace Mechanism
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: Our unbiased estimator achieves far lower error and bias than the naive estimator on real datasets across privacy levels.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; left log-log error band plot, right stacked profile and error plots
description: Two side-by-side plot panels show real-data results for the naive estimator versus the unbiased estimator. Panel (a) is a log-log plot of normalized RMSE against epsilon on the NIPS bag-of-words entropy task. A red naive-estimator median line with a pink 10th-90th percentile band sits well above a blue unbiased-estimator median line with a lavender band. The gap is roughly one to two orders of magnitude, and both lines slope downward as epsilon grows. Panel (b) shows profile estimation on the ExAC histogram at epsilon=1. The top plot is the fraction of elements against frequency k. It has a black true-profile curve, with an orange dashed naive mean that deviates at k=1 and green and blue unbiased and central means that overlay the truth. The bottom plot is mean fraction error. The orange naive error dips to about -0.27 at k=1, while the green and blue errors stay flat near zero. The eye goes first to the red and blue bands on the left.
caption: Examples where our estimator compares favorably to the naive estimator on real datasets.
abstract: We show that an "old dog," the classical discrete Laplace (aka. geometric) mechanism, can "perform new tricks": * It can be post-processed to yield a simple, unbiased estimator of any subexponential function $f$ of the original data, giving a simple, discrete, multivariate version of the recent unbiasing result for the Laplace mechanism by Calmon et al. (FORC '25). * It can be post-processed to output the same distribution as the Laplace mechanism or the Staircase mechanism with identical privacy parameters. Thus, the discrete Laplace mechanism is a versatile mechanism that should be preferred over the Laplace and Staircase mechanisms whenever the data is discrete. We show bounds on the variance of our estimator, compared to the mean square error of the biased estimator that simply evaluates $f$ on the output of the mechanism. Though our unbiased estimator has exponential running time for worst-case functions, we show that it can often be computed in linear or polynomial time for some common functions exhibiting structure. We showcase the properties of our methods empirically with several use cases including profile and entropy estimation, as well as distributed/federated data analysis applications in which unbiasedness is key to accuracy.
